# How to Generate Images with Google Gemini: A Beginner's Guide

> **In short:** Yes, Gemini can generate images. On a computer, go to gemini.google.com, click **Open Sidebar**, then **Images**, and describe the picture you want. Gemini draws it with Google's Nano Banana models, and you can edit it, download it or send it to Google Docs.

Need a party invitation, an illustration for a slide, or a silly picture of your dog dressed as a pirate? You don't need design software for that. Gemini, Google's AI assistant, has a built-in image generator, and you ask it for pictures the same way you'd ask a friend. This guide follows Google's own help page for the feature, so the button names below are the ones Google documents.

## Before you start

- **A Google Account, signed in to Gemini.** Image generation only works when you're signed in.
- **The right age.** With a personal account, you must be 13 or older (or the minimum age in your country) to create images, and 18 or older to edit them. School accounts may have extra limits.
- **A supported country and language.** Like every Gemini feature, image generation is limited to the languages and countries where the Gemini app is available.
- **A computer with a web browser.** The steps below are for gemini.google.com. The Gemini app on Android and iPhone makes images too, but its menus are laid out a little differently; Google's help page has a separate tab for each.
- **About 10 minutes.**

## Step 1 — Open the Images page in Gemini

Go to `gemini.google.com` and sign in. In the top-left corner, click **Open Sidebar**, then click **Images**.

You'll see a choice of ready-made templates and a box for your own **prompt** (the written instruction you give an AI). Templates are a handy shortcut when you're not sure what to ask for.

**You'll know it worked when** the Images page shows the template choices and a text box ready for you to type.

**If it looks different:** if you don't see **Images** in the sidebar, check that you're signed in and that you meet the age requirement above. The feature may also not be offered in your country or language yet.

## Step 2 — Write your first prompt

Pick a template, or type your own request. Google's tips for a good image prompt come down to three things:

1. **Start with an action word** such as *draw*, *generate* or *create*, so Gemini knows you want a picture, not a written answer.
2. **Name a style**, for example *photorealistic*, *charcoal drawing*, *watercolor painting* or *cartoon illustration*.
3. **Describe the scene in detail:** the subject, what it's doing, and the background or setting.

Then send your prompt.

💬 **Example prompt to copy:**
> "Create a watercolor painting of a golden retriever puppy with a red collar, sitting on a sunny lawn next to a yellow tennis ball."

**You'll know it worked when** an image that matches your description appears in the conversation.

**If it looks different:** if Gemini answers with text instead of a picture, send a new message that starts with "Create an image of…" and repeat your description.

## Step 3 — Add a reference photo (optional)

You can upload images as a reference when you ask for a new picture. For example, upload a photo of your living room and ask Gemini to "draw this room in a cozy winter style." Google says its image models keep a subject consistent across images, so this is also how you put the same pet or character into several different scenes.

Attach the photo the same way you'd attach any file in Gemini, then type your prompt.

**You'll know it worked when** the new image clearly uses details from the photo you uploaded.

## Step 4 — Edit an image you made

Editing is available to people 18 and older. To change an image you already created:

1. Click **Open Sidebar**, then **Library**.
2. Find the image and click it.
3. Under the image, click **Chat**.
4. In the text box at the bottom, describe the change you want.
5. Click **Submit**.

You can also upload one of your own photos and ask Gemini to edit it, or upload several images and ask for a new picture based on all of them.

💬 **Example edit request:**
> "Make the sky bluer and add a small sailboat on the horizon."

**You'll know it worked when** Gemini shows a new version of the image with the change you asked for.

## Step 5 — Download your image or send it to Google Docs

- **To download it:** hover over the image and click **Download full size**.
- **To put it in a document:** under the image, click **More**, then **Export to Docs**. Open the new doc to keep working on it.

A downloaded image is an ordinary picture file you can drop into slides, emails or social posts.

**You'll know it worked when** the file shows up in your computer's Downloads folder, or a new Google Doc opens with your image inside.

## Want more detail? Redo it with Nano Banana Pro

If you have a Google AI plan, you can ask for a more detailed version of an image, which helps most with pictures that contain text and with infographics. At the bottom right of the image, click **More**, then **Redo with Pro**. Google notes one catch: once you reach your daily limit for regular images, you can't redo any more images with Pro.

Which Nano Banana model draws your picture depends on the Gemini model you've selected. To use a different one, switch your Gemini model before you write the image request.

## Common mistakes

- **Being too vague.** "A cat" gives you a random cat. "A sleepy tabby cat curled up on a blue knitted blanket by a fireplace, cartoon illustration" gives Gemini something to work with.
- **Forgetting the action word.** Without *create*, *draw* or *generate*, Gemini may describe a picture in words instead of drawing it.
- **Avoiding text in images.** Older image tools mangled words, but Google says Nano Banana renders text accurately. If you want a headline on a poster or a name on a card, include the exact words in your prompt.
- **Expecting every image to stay.** Gemini may remove an image if Google's systems detect a possible violation of its Terms of Service, including the Prohibited Use Policy. Don't use other people's photos or copyrighted characters without permission.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** make one-off birthday cards, party invitations and phone wallpapers, or see yourself with a new hairstyle before you visit the salon.
- **For work or a small business:** create simple illustrations for slides, blog posts and social updates, and send them straight to Google Docs while you draft.
- **If you're just getting started:** begin with a template, then borrow its wording for your own prompts. Changing one thing at a time, like a single style word or one extra detail, teaches you more than starting over.

Before you publish anything, take a second look: Google asks users to use their judgment before relying on or sharing content that Gemini creates.

## Try it now

Open Gemini, click **Open Sidebar**, then **Images**, and paste this prompt:

> "Create a cheerful cartoon illustration of a koala holding a warm cup of tea, with the words 'Good Morning' in big, friendly letters."
